channel.description: Recent content in events on Japan Specialty Traveler

item.title: Aichi Events 2026: Nagoya Sumo, Fireworks, Tenno Festival & Ghibli Park
item.description: Aichi — with Nagoya at its heart — is the manufacturing engine of Japan, but its 2026 event calendar is pure summer spectacle and samurai heritage. The prefecture hosts a July Grand Sumo tournament in a brand-new arena, some of the country’s biggest fireworks in its “Mikawa fireworks” heartland, a 600-year-old UNESCO river festival, a procession of the three warlords who unified Japan, and Studio Ghibli’s own theme park. This guide gathers the events worth planning a 2026 trip around, with a month-by-month calendar at the end.

item.title: Akita Events 2026: Kanto Festival, Omagari Fireworks & Namahage
item.description: Akita’s calendar swings between two extremes: a summer of luminous festivals and Japan’s most prestigious fireworks, and a deep winter of snow igloos and demon rituals. The Kanto Festival’s forests of balanced lantern-poles are one of Tohoku’s three great summer festivals; the Omagari competition is where Japan’s top pyrotechnicians battle for the national crown; and in February, the Oga Peninsula’s Namahage demons and Yokote’s candle-lit snow huts define northern winter. This guide gathers the events worth planning a 2026 trip around, with a month-by-month calendar at the end.

item.title: Fukuoka Events 2026: Yamakasa, Dontaku, Kanmon Fireworks & Kyushu Sumo
item.description: Fukuoka wears its festival culture on its sleeve. Hakata — the old merchant heart of the city — hosts two of Kyushu’s most explosive festivals within months of each other (Dontaku in May, Yamakasa in July), the region’s only Grand Sumo tournament arrives each November, and one of Japan’s biggest fireworks displays lights up the Kanmon Strait in August. Add a week-long autumn shrine festival famous for its food stalls, and Fukuoka’s 2026 calendar rewards a well-timed trip.

item.title: Gifu Events 2026: Takayama Festival, Gujo Odori & Cormorant Fishing
item.description: Gifu’s mountainous heart hosts some of Japan’s most refined and enduring traditions. The Takayama Festival’s ornate automaton floats are counted among the country’s most beautiful; Gujo Odori is a dance the whole town joins for two months, culminating in four all-night sessions; and on the Nagara River, cormorant fishing has continued unbroken for 1,300 years. Add the winter magic of Shirakawa-go’s illuminated thatched village, and Gifu rewards a well-timed 2026 trip.

item.title: Kagawa Events 2026: Takamatsu Festival Fireworks, Konpira & Art Islands
item.description: Kagawa, Japan’s smallest prefecture, punches far above its size — home of Sanuki udon, the pilgrimage shrine of Konpira-san, the celebrated Ritsurin Garden, and the “art islands” of the Seto Inland Sea. Its 2026 event calendar centres on a lively summer festival with fireworks over Takamatsu’s harbour, alongside year-round island art and one of Japan’s finest strolling gardens. This guide gathers the events worth planning a 2026 trip around, with a month-by-month calendar at the end.

item.title: Kagoshima Events 2026: Kinko Bay Fireworks, Ohara Matsuri & Sakurajima
item.description: Kagoshima lives in the shadow of Sakurajima, one of the world’s most active volcanoes, which smokes across the bay from the city every day. Its 2026 event calendar matches that drama: Kyushu’s largest fireworks display over Kinko Bay, southern Japan’s biggest street dance festival, and the year-round spectacle of the volcano itself. Add the steaming sand baths of Ibusuki and the ancient forests of Yakushima offshore, and Kagoshima rewards a well-timed 2026 trip.

item.title: Kanagawa Events 2026: Yokohama Fireworks, Tanabata & Hakone Parade
item.description: Kanagawa packs an unusual variety into one prefecture: the harbour glamour of Yokohama, the temples and beaches of Kamakura and Shonan, and the mountain onsen of Hakone. Its 2026 event calendar is just as varied — near-monthly fireworks over Yokohama’s port, one of the Kanto region’s three great Tanabata festivals, a feudal-lord procession through Hakone, and horseback archery at Kamakura’s great shrine. This guide gathers the events worth planning a 2026 trip around, with a month-by-month calendar at the end.

item.title: Mie Events 2026: Ise Fireworks, Kumano Fireworks & Ueno Tenjin
item.description: Mie is the spiritual heart of Japan — home to Ise Jingu, the most sacred of all Shinto shrines — and its 2026 event calendar blends the sacred with the spectacular. Two of the country’s finest fireworks displays light up the Ise river and the Kumano sea within a month of each other; a ninja-country festival parades through Iga; and one of Japan’s largest winter illuminations glows at Nabana no Sato.

item.title: Nagano Events 2026: Nozawa Fire Festival, Suwa Fireworks & Snow Monkeys
item.description: Nagano’s events run with its mountains and seasons: a fiery midwinter ritual in a snowbound onsen village, one of Japan’s largest fireworks displays over a mountain lake, the famous macaques bathing in steaming pools, and cherry blossoms so celebrated they draw crowds to a former castle in the hills. This guide gathers the events worth planning a 2026 trip around, with a month-by-month calendar at the end. A note on dates: Confirmed 2026 dates are given where announced.

item.title: Nagasaki Events 2026: Lantern Festival, Kunchi & Shoro Nagashi
item.description: Nagasaki’s centuries as Japan’s window to China and the West shaped an event calendar unlike anywhere else in the country. The Lantern Festival fills the city with 15,000 Chinese lanterns each February; the Kunchi festival blends Japanese, Chinese, and Dutch influences into a spectacular autumn procession; and the deeply moving August 9 Peace Ceremony and the firecracker-lit Shoro Nagashi spirit boats give the summer a solemn power. This guide gathers the events worth planning a 2026 trip around, with a month-by-month calendar at the end.

item.title: Oita Events 2026: Beppu Fireworks, Onsen Festival & Usuki Takeyoi
item.description: Oita is Japan’s onsen capital — Beppu and Yufuin between them pour out more hot-spring water than anywhere else in the country — and its 2026 event calendar reflects that steamy character. A spring festival celebrates the hot springs themselves, summer brings fireworks over Beppu Bay, and autumn glows with thousands of bamboo lanterns in a castle town. Add the ever-bubbling “hells” of Beppu, and Oita rewards a well-timed 2026 trip.

item.title: Okayama Events 2026: Saidaiji Naked Festival, Momotaro & Korakuen
item.description: Okayama — the sunny “Land of Sunshine” on the Seto Inland Sea — mixes one of Japan’s wildest winter rituals with the serene beauty of a great garden. In February, thousands of men in loincloths battle for lucky sticks in near-darkness at Saidaiji; in summer, a festival named for the folk hero Momotaro fills the city with dance and fireworks; and year-round, the celebrated Korakuen garden glows with seasonal illuminations. This guide gathers the events worth planning a 2026 trip around, with a month-by-month calendar at the end.

item.title: Shiga Events 2026: Biwako Fireworks, Otsu Matsuri & Sagicho
item.description: Shiga wraps around Lake Biwa, Japan’s largest lake, and its 2026 event calendar plays out on and around the water: one of the Kansai region’s biggest fireworks displays over the lake in Otsu, a rare simultaneous show fired from three shores, and a set of centuries-old festivals in the historic towns that ring it. Add spring blossoms over the water and autumn colour at ancient temples, and Shiga rewards a well-timed 2026 trip.

item.title: Tokushima Events 2026: Awa Odori, Fireworks & Machi Asobi
item.description: Tokushima’s event calendar is defined by one of the most electrifying festivals on earth. For four August nights, the whole city of Tokushima becomes a stage for the Awa Odori — 400 years of dance, drums, and the cry of “fools dancing, fools watching, so dance!” Around it, the prefecture offers the roaring Naruto whirlpools at their spring peak, a twice-yearly anime festival that takes over the city, and the deep-mountain quiet of the Iya Valley.

item.title: Tokyo Events 2026: Festivals, Fireworks & One-Off Happenings
item.description: Tokyo runs on a calendar of its own. In any given month, the city is hosting a centuries-old shrine festival, a national sumo tournament, a fireworks display drawing a million spectators, a pop-culture collaboration that exists only in 2026, and a seasonal spectacle timed to the blossoms or the autumn leaves. This guide gathers the events worth planning a 2026 trip around — the fixed annual traditions, the summer fireworks, and the one-off happenings you can only catch this year — with a month-by-month calendar at the end.

item.title: Saitama Super Arena: Japan's Massive Multi-Purpose Venue — Guide
item.description: Saitama Super Arena is one of the largest multi-purpose indoor arenas in Asia, its distinctive design featuring a movable main stand that allows the venue to reconfigure between a compact arena setting and a massive stadium-style space seating up to roughly 37,000. Since opening in 2000, it has hosted major international concerts, world championship sporting events, conventions and the wrestling and basketball events of the Tokyo 2020 Olympics, making it a key stop for visitors attending large-scale events near Tokyo.

item.title: Dotonbori Halloween Guide: What It's Really Like in Osaka
item.description: Around October 31, costumed crowds gather in and around Dotonbori for an informal Halloween street party — Osaka’s equivalent of Tokyo’s Shibuya scramble. It’s spontaneous and unofficial: there’s no organised event, no stage, no tickets — just thousands of people in costume filling the Ebisubashi bridge and Dotonbori canalside to see and be seen. It can be fun and photogenic, but it’s also extremely crowded and increasingly managed by police. Here’s an honest picture of what it’s actually like and how to do it sensibly — plus better alternatives.

item.title: Makuhari Messe Guide: Events, Expos & Access
item.description: Makuhari Messe, in the Bayfront business district of Chiba, is one of Japan’s largest convention and exhibition centres — and a magnet for international fans of Japanese pop culture. Designed by architect Fumihiko Maki and opened in 1989, its vast halls and event arena host an extraordinary calendar: blockbuster anime, manga and gaming expos, music concerts and festivals, motor and tech trade shows, and major sporting events. For overseas visitors, it’s the venue behind many bucket-list events, and its location between Tokyo and Narita Airport — with a cluster of hotels, malls and a beach park nearby — makes it remarkably convenient to attend.

item.title: Shibuya Halloween: What's Really Happening Now (Honest Guide)
item.description: For years, Shibuya’s Halloween was famous as one of the world’s largest spontaneous costume gatherings — tens of thousands of revellers in elaborate outfits flooding the scramble crossing with no organiser, no tickets, just an enormous self-generating street party. If you’ve read older travel guides, that’s the image they sell. Here’s the honest, current reality: Shibuya no longer wants this, and is actively asking people — especially crowds and tourists — to stay away on Halloween.

item.title: Hiroshima Events 2026: Peace Ceremony, Flower Festival, Kangensai & Fireworks
item.description: Hiroshima’s event calendar is unusually wide in tone. The August 6 Peace Memorial Ceremony is one of the world’s most significant annual commemorations; the Kangensai boat festival on Miyajima is one of Japan’s oldest and most atmospheric Shinto rituals; the Flower Festival draws over a million people during Golden Week. Add summer fireworks over the bay, a legendary sake festival, and a beloved baseball team, and Hiroshima rewards a well-timed 2026 trip.

item.title: Comiket 2026 Survival Guide: How to Visit Comic Market
item.description: Every year, twice a year, the attention of the anime and manga world swings to a cluster of futuristic buildings on the waterfront of Tokyo Bay. Over three days, more than 700,000 fans pour into Tokyo Big Sight for Comiket — the world’s largest self-published media fair, where over 30,000 independent creator groups (circles) sell their own original comics, art books, games, and music directly to buyers. If Akihabara is anime culture’s permanent home, Comiket is its beating heart.

item.title: Wakayama Events & Festivals: Fire Festivals, Plum Blossom Season & Traditional Celebrations
item.description: Wakayama’s festival calendar is shaped by two things that define the prefecture itself: ancient religious tradition and agricultural cycle. The Kumano Grand Shrines have been hosting ritual ceremonies without interruption for over 1,500 years; the mountain valleys have been marking planting, harvest, and the seasons with community events for as long as anyone can trace. The result is a calendar of genuinely un-performed events — festivals that exist because communities have always done them, not because a tourism board decided a festival would attract visitors.

item.title: Aomori Events & Festivals: Nebuta, Hirosaki Cherry Blossoms & Hachinohe Emburi
item.description: Aomori Prefecture Events and Festivals Guide for International Visitors Aomori Prefecture, occupying Japan’s northernmost point on Honshu, hosts some of the nation’s most spectacular and unique festivals. From explosive summer celebrations to mystical winter rituals, these events offer international visitors authentic cultural experiences far removed from typical tourist circuits. 1. Aomori Nebuta Festival (August 2–7) Overview The Aomori Nebuta Festival ranks among Japan’s three greatest festivals (alongside Sendai Tanabata and Akita Kanto), drawing approximately three million spectators annually.

item.title: Fukushima Events & Festivals: Soma Nomaoi Wild Horse Festival, Nebuta & Aizu Matsuri
item.description: Fukushima Prefecture Events and Festivals Guide for International Visitors Fukushima Prefecture’s festival calendar reflects the full range of its cultural identity: ancient equestrian martial arts on the Pacific coast, samurai pageantry in the castle town of Aizu, stone lanterns transforming a hillside castle in the autumn night, and a single cherry tree drawing thousands to pay quiet respects in spring. These festivals are not tourist productions—they are community expressions of heritage that happen to welcome outside observers.

item.title: Iwate Events & Festivals: Chagu-Chagu Umakko, Sansa Odori & Hiraizumi Pageants
item.description: Iwate Prefecture Events and Festivals Guide for International Visitors Iwate Prefecture, Japan’s second-largest prefecture by area, offers visitors a rich tapestry of cultural festivals that showcase centuries-old traditions, stunning natural beauty, and the warm hospitality of the Tohoku region. From thunderous drum parades to sacred horse processions, these events provide unforgettable windows into northern Japan’s heritage. Chagu-Chagu Umakko: The Jingling Horse Parade When: Second Saturday of June (typically June 8-14)

item.title: Miyagi Events & Festivals: Sendai Tanabata, Pageant of Starlight & Matsushima Fireworks
item.description: Miyagi Prefecture Events and Festivals Guide for International Visitors Miyagi Prefecture, anchored by the dynamic city of Sendai and graced by the ethereal beauty of Matsushima Bay, hosts some of Japan’s most spectacular festivals and seasonal events. From the cascading paper streamers of Tanabata to winter illuminations and sacred maritime processions, Miyagi’s event calendar offers international visitors profound cultural experiences paired with natural beauty. Here’s your comprehensive guide to planning around the prefecture’s major annual celebrations.

item.title: Niigata Events & Festivals: Kodo Earth Celebration, Sake no Jin & Snow Country Winter
item.description: Niigata Prefecture Events and Festivals Guide for International Visitors Niigata Prefecture, stretching along the Sea of Japan coast, offers a calendar of exceptional cultural events that reflect its identity as a snow country, sake heartland, and artistic frontier. From world-class taiko drumming on remote islands to Japan’s largest sake gathering, these festivals provide entry points into traditions that have shaped this region for centuries. Major Annual Events Kodo Earth Celebration (鼓童アース・セレブレーション) When: Mid-to-late August (3 days)

item.title: Toyama Events & Festivals: Owara Kaze-no-Bon, Snow Corridor Opening & Kurobe Gorge Autumn
item.description: Toyama’s event calendar is anchored by experiences that have taken generations to refine. The dance festival at Yatsuo is considered one of Japan’s most aesthetically perfect festivals; the alpine snow corridor opening each April is one of the country’s most visually dramatic seasonal events; and the last trains of the Kurobe Gorge season in November close out the year with foliage colour that is among the finest in Hokuriku. Owara Kaze-no-Bon (September 1–3) Owara Kaze-no-Bon is held each year in the mountain town of Yatsuo, about 25 kilometres south of Toyama City.

item.title: Yamagata Events & Festivals: Hanagasa Matsuri, Imoni Feast & Snow Monster Season
item.description: Yamagata Prefecture Events and Festivals Guide for International Visitors Yamagata Prefecture, nestled in the Tohoku region of northern Japan, offers visitors a remarkable calendar of festivals and seasonal events that showcase both traditional culture and extraordinary natural phenomena. From massive food festivals to human chess matches and supernatural snow formations, Yamagata’s events provide experiences found nowhere else in Japan. Yamagata Hanagasa Matsuri (August 5–7) The Hanagasa Festival is Yamagata City’s marquee summer celebration and one of Tohoku’s four great festivals.

item.title: Fukui Events & Festivals: Mikuni Festival, Crab Festivals & Lantern Nights
item.description: Fukui Prefecture’s festival calendar reflects the character of the region itself: deeply rooted in local tradition, uninterested in performance for outside audiences, and genuinely spectacular when encountered on its own terms. The festivals here have been running for centuries in some cases, sustained not by tourism infrastructure but by the communities that have always organized and participated in them. The Mikuni Festival’s enormous floats are built and maintained by neighborhood associations that take this responsibility entirely seriously across generations.

item.title: Hyogo Events & Festivals: Himeji Cherry Blossoms, Kobe Luminarie & Sake Matsuri
item.description: Hyogo Prefecture’s festival calendar reflects the full range of what makes the region culturally distinctive: refined urban spectacles in Kobe, ancient shrine rituals in the castle towns, the seasonal rhythms of the Sea of Japan fishing coast, and the sake-brewing traditions that have defined the Nada district for four centuries. The prefecture is also home to arguably Japan’s most photographed castle at arguably Japan’s most photogenic time of year — which alone gives Hyogo a claim on the attention of visitors timing their trip around the spring cherry blossom season.

item.title: Shimane Events & Festivals: Kamiarisai, Peony Season & Seasonal Celebrations
item.description: Shimane’s event calendar is shaped by one fact that sets this prefecture apart from every other in Japan: when the rest of the country calls October “Kannazuki” (the month without gods), Shimane calls it “Kamiarisuki” — the month WITH gods. All 8 million deities of Japan are believed to gather at Izumo Taisha during this period, making Shimane the religious center of the country for roughly a month each autumn.

item.title: Tottori Events & Festivals: Shan-Shan Umbrella Dance, Crab Season & Seasonal Celebrations
item.description: Tottori is quiet by Japanese standards — that’s one of its virtues. But several times a year the prefecture comes alive with events that are genuinely worth planning a trip around. The Shan-Shan umbrella festival is one of Japan’s most distinctive summer celebrations. Matsuba crab season opening in November is a spectacle with real ritual attached to it. And the sand dunes at night, lit by seasonal illuminations, are something you can’t see anywhere else in the world.

item.title: Chiba Events 2026: Fireworks, Tokyo Game Show, Gion Festivals & Disney
item.description: Chiba is where most visitors land (Narita Airport) and where Tokyo Disney Resort actually sits — but the prefecture’s own 2026 event calendar is far richer than a transit stop suggests. It hosts some of the Kanto region’s biggest summer fireworks, two UNESCO-linked Gion float festivals on the same weekend, the world’s largest video-game show, a temple-steps display of thirty thousand hina dolls, and whale-and-dolphin watching off its Pacific coast. This guide gathers the events worth planning a 2026 trip around, with a month-by-month calendar at the end.

item.title: Yamanashi Events & Festivals: Shibazakura, Wine Festival & Yoshida Fire
item.description: Yamanashi’s event calendar is dictated by the mountain and the vine — seasonal festivals that draw hundreds of thousands of visitors are choreographed around Mt Fuji’s changing appearance across the year. The pink flower fields of spring, the harvest celebrations of autumn, the fire rituals of late summer: each is tied intimately to the landscape and the agricultural cycles that have sustained this landlocked prefecture for centuries. Fuji Kawaguchiko Shibazakura Festival (Late April–Late May) The Fuji Kawaguchiko Shibazakura Festival is one of Japan’s most spectacular flower events and without question the most famous sight in Yamanashi outside of Mt Fuji itself.

item.title: Nara Events & Festivals 2026: Lanterns, Deer Ceremonies & Ancient Rituals
item.description: Nara’s festival calendar is one of the richest in Japan — not because it has manufactured tourist events, but because many of the ceremonies here are among the oldest continuously observed religious rituals in the world. The Omizutori water-drawing ceremony at Todai-ji has been performed every year since 752 AD without interruption. The Kasuga Taisha Mantoro lantern festival lights the same 3,000 lanterns that have been donated across 1,000 years. The annual deer antler cutting is a direct continuation of the tradition that has protected both deer and people since the 8th century.

item.title: Ehime Events & Festivals: Niihama Taiko, Matsuyama Autumn & Uwajima Ushi-oni
item.description: Ehime’s festival calendar is anchored at one end by one of the largest and most physically intense portable shrine festivals in all of Japan, and at the other by a winter onsen illumination that turns the country’s oldest hot spring building into something from a fever dream. Between those poles, bull-demons rampage through Uwajima, Matsuyama fills with dancers, and the Seto Inland Sea reflects summer fireworks from the bridges of Shimanami Kaido.

item.title: Gunma Events & Festivals Calendar
item.description: Gunma’s festival calendar is anchored by a handful of genuinely distinctive events — Japan’s largest daruma fair, a marsh that turns white with skunk cabbage in early June, volcanic lake foliage in October — alongside the slower seasonal rhythms that make the prefecture rewarding to visit in any month. This guide covers the full year, with practical notes on timing, crowds, and access. Winter (December to February) Winter is one of Gunma’s most atmospheric seasons.

item.title: Ibaraki Events & Festivals Calendar
item.description: Ibaraki is one of those prefectures that rewards visitors who time their trip to the season. Come at the wrong time of year and you will find pleasant but unremarkable farmland and coastal towns. Come at the right time and you will encounter one of Japan’s great plum blossom festivals, a hillside of 4.5 million blue nemophila flowers, a crimson landscape of kochia balls in October, or a samurai parade through a city with a 300-year connection to Japan’s most beloved historical drama.

item.title: Kochi Events & Festivals: Yosakoi, Tosa Reihoku & Whale Watching Season
item.description: Kochi’s festival calendar runs almost year-round, anchored by one of Japan’s most exuberant modern festivals in summer, a set of ancient agricultural rituals in winter, and a whale-watching season that draws visitors from spring through autumn. The prefecture’s distance from the main tourist circuits means that even the major events can be experienced without the overcrowding that affects festivals in Kyoto or Tokyo. Yosakoi Festival (August 9–12) If there is a single festival in Kochi that defines the prefecture’s character, it is the Yosakoi.

item.title: Okinawa Festivals Guide: Eisa, Dragon Boats, Lanterns & Ryukyuan Ceremonies
item.description: Okinawa’s festival calendar reflects its unique heritage — Ryukyuan religious ceremonies, Obon customs distinct from mainland Japan, and a performance tradition centred on the eisa drum dance and sanshin music that has no equivalent anywhere else. The events are not recreations for tourists; they are living community traditions. 旧盆エイサー — Okinawan Eisa (Obon Period) When: Three days of Obon by the lunar calendar — typically mid-to-late August Where: Every village and neighbourhood across Okinawa; biggest in Okinawa City (Koza)

item.title: Saitama Events 2026: Chichibu Night Festival, Kawagoe Matsuri & Fireworks
item.description: Just north of Tokyo, Saitama is an easy day trip that hides two of Japan’s most important festivals. The Chichibu Night Festival and the Kawagoe Matsuri are both UNESCO-recognised float processions, and the prefecture also stages a Guinness-record firework, a hillside of half a million moss-phlox blooms, and the “Little Edo” charm of Kawagoe’s warehouse district. This guide gathers the events worth planning a 2026 trip around, with a month-by-month calendar at the end.

item.title: Tochigi Events & Festivals Calendar
item.description: Tochigi Prefecture has an events calendar that rewards careful timing. The region’s two headline festivals are among the most theatrical in eastern Japan — a thousand warriors in full Edo-period armor marching through Nikko’s cedar forest, and enormous carved wooden floats rolling through a historic warehouse townscape. Alongside these, the seasons bring cherry blossoms, pottery markets, hydrangeas, vivid autumn foliage, and winter strawberries. Whatever time of year you plan to visit, there is something worth planning around.

item.title: Hokkaido Events 2026: Snow Festival, Yosakoi Soran, Lavender & Fireworks
item.description: Hokkaido’s events follow its dramatic seasons. Winter brings the snow-and-ice spectacle the island is world-famous for — the Sapporo Snow Festival and a string of candle-lit and ice-carved events across the region. Then summer flips the script entirely: energetic street dancing in June, lavender fields and hillside fireworks in July, and one of Japan’s great food festivals in autumn. This guide gathers the events worth planning a 2026 trip around, with a month-by-month calendar at the end.

item.title: Osaka Events 2026: Festivals, Fireworks, Sumo & USJ Happenings
item.description: Osaka does festivals the way it does everything — loud, warm, and food-first. The city’s 2026 calendar runs from one of Japan’s three great festivals (Tenjin Matsuri, with its river-boat procession and fireworks) to the heart-stopping cart races of Kishiwada Danjiri, a spring Grand Sumo tournament, the year’s biggest anime collaborations at Universal Studios Japan, and a cherry-blossom tunnel opened for just one week. This guide gathers the events worth planning a 2026 trip around, with a month-by-month calendar at the end.

item.title: Kyoto Events 2026: Gion Matsuri, the Three Great Festivals & Seasonal Light-Ups
item.description: No city in Japan keeps its festival calendar the way Kyoto does. The former capital hosts three of the country’s most storied processions — Aoi, Gion, and Jidai — each a living re-enactment of the imperial and medieval past, alongside a mountainside bonfire seen for miles, a torch-lit fire festival in the northern hills, private geisha dances, and seasonal temple light-ups timed to the cherry blossoms and autumn maples. This guide gathers the events worth planning a 2026 trip around, with a month-by-month calendar at the end.

item.title: Ishikawa Events & Festivals: Hyakumangoku, Wajima Kiriko & More
item.description: Ishikawa Events & Festivals: The Complete Annual Calendar Ishikawa Prefecture punches well above its weight in cultural events. Its capital, Kanazawa, was the seat of the Maeda clan — the wealthiest domain outside the Tokugawa shogunate — and those centuries of aristocratic patronage produced a legacy of Noh theatre, traditional music, and annual festivals that the city maintains with remarkable fidelity. Beyond Kanazawa, the Noto Peninsula carries its own ancient festival traditions, centred on the spectacular illuminated lantern processions known as kiriko.

item.title: Osaka in October 2026 Autumn Weather Guide Events
item.description: Osaka in October: Weather, Events & What to Do — The Ultimate Autumn Guide October is when Osaka finally exhales. After months of punishing summer humidity that can leave even the hardiest traveler wilting, the city transforms into something magical — crisp mornings, golden afternoon light, and a culinary scene that shifts into high gear with autumn harvests. If you’re researching Osaka in October weather events what to do, you’ve landed on the best possible month to experience Japan’s second city.
